title: Sealed vault inference capacity & update process discovery - Cedar River Labs
topics: fallback and canary strategies for offline nodes
summary: Initial discovery for fully isolated inference deployment. Customer operates in a regulated lab environment; primary concerns were update delivery in an air-gapped facility, hardware constraints (Pascal/Turing era GPUs, limited NVMe), and auditability for auditors. Redwood AE/SE walked through private deployment modes, offline patch processes (signed images, USB + signature verification), model pinning, and a proposed minimal POC of a 1-node cluster. Next steps: share security pack, HW checklist, schedule on-site inventory and an SE deep-dive for firmware signing and test harness.

transcript:
Meeting header: Date: 2027-06-14; Start: 17:30 PDT; Duration: 48 min; Recording id: frf-20270614-cedarriver-01

[00:00] Alyssa (Redwood AE): Hi everyone, Alyssa here from Redwood, thanks for carving out the time. Jamal's on the call as well, our SE. How's everybody doing?
[00:10] Dr. Maya (CTO): Good, thanks. Busy week but excited to dig in.
[00:14] Ethan (Security): Hi, Ethan here. We'll hear a lot about policy, sorry in advance.
[00:18] Rosa (Infra): Rosa on infra, I have a spreadsheet of hosts if that helps later.
[00:23] Jamal (Redwood SE): Hey team, quick agenda — confirm constraints, update cadence, hardware capabilities, and what a pilot could look like.
[00:30] Alyssa: Great, can we start with the network posture? Are you fully disconnected or is there a dimly connected staging network?
[00:38] Dr. Maya: Fully sealed. No egress from the compute cluster. We have a separate staging lab with pull-only USB transfer windows. Auditors require no internet footprint on production nodes.
[00:48] Jamal: Got it. So an air-gapped/private install. Two immediate questions — how do you want updates delivered (sneakernet, removable media) and what hardware are we working with?
[00:58] Rosa: Mostly older cards — we have a mix: 2 x V100s, some T4s, couple of GTX 1080/1080 Ti in edge racks. Storage is constrained: 1 TB NVMe per host in most places.
[01:15] Ethan: Also encryption questions — we use a local HSM in the data center but it's offline. We cannot have cloud KMS calls.
[01:24] Alyssa: Makes sense. Redwood Private supports on-prem with a local KMS/HSM integration and we can do an image-based update model. Our recommended pattern for fully sealed sites is signed images delivered on removable media and verified by the node's bootloader, then the runtime applies the model artifact locally.
[01:41] Dr. Maya: Signed images, so the node verifies signatures and won't run unsigned code?
[01:46] Jamal: Exactly. We sign both the runtime binary bundles and the model shards. Verification is done with an on-site public key held in an HSM or TPM. No outbound network is required during verification.
[01:58] Ethan: How does that work with model pinning? We need reproducible hashes for the auditors.
[02:03] Jamal: We produce an artifact manifest with SHA-256 hashes for every model shard and runtime version. The manifest itself is also signed. So auditors can confirm the SHA and the signature chain.
[02:15] Rosa: Cool. But our hosts have limited NVMe; what's the working set requirement? Can we stream from an NFS or do we need full shard local copy?
[02:25] Jamal: Streaming is possible but in a sealed env they prefer local copies to avoid runtime network needs. For typical LLMs, with model quantization (8-bit or 4-bit) we can fit smaller models — but larger ones will need either model sharding across nodes or NVMe-backed mmap. If you only have 1 TB you might fit a 7B-13B quantized profile, depending on tokenizer cache and kv sizes.
[02:47] Dr. Maya: We were hoping to run a variant of the open model you guys recommend. Is there a pre-quantized artifact or do you help with quantization onsite?
[02:56] Jamal: We have recommended quantization profiles and can provide pre-quantized model artifacts as part of the POC. We also provide tooling to re-quantize in a controlled environment; for sealed sites we typically do that in your staging lab and then sign the artifacts.
[03:10] Alyssa: Timeline question: how long before auditors and product teams are comfortable to approve a pilot?
[03:14] Dr. Maya: Conservatively 6–9 months, but if you can show a tight signed-image runbook and a short pilot that proves signing and rollback, maybe 3–4 months.
[03:24] Ethan: One big ask — our compliance team requires proof of rollback and read-only artifacts after install. How does Redwood handle rollbacks if an update fails mid-deploy and there's no net access to fetch fallback?
[03:36] Jamal: Our runtime supports atomic swaps — the bootloader mounts the new image to a slot, verifies signature, switches the active slot on successful health checks. If the new slot fails health checks the bootloader switches back to the previous slot. All artifacts are kept in an encrypted read-only partition until overwritten by a signed image.
[03:52] Rosa: Ok that sounds promising. What about telemetry? We can't send usage telemetry out of the sealed env, but we do need logs for internal ops and audits.
[04:01] Alyssa: We support local logging and an audit bundle export. You can export logs as a signed tarball and provide them to auditors manually. We can also include a remote proxy mode for non-production staging if you ever allow it.
[04:14] Dr. Maya: Can you talk about model updates frequency? We prefer quarterly model refreshes but security updates might be monthly.
[04:21] Jamal: That's typical. The process we recommend: (1) Redwood produces signed security patches (runtime) monthly, (2) model updates quarterly or as needed. For the POC we'll scope one runtime update and one model refresh to exercise the full flow.
[04:35] Ethan: Are there any dependencies that still need outbound access at some point — e.g. license checks?
[04:40] Alyssa: No. Our Private mode can operate fully offline. Licensing checks are handled by the license token baked into the signed bundle; validation occurs locally. The license token is time-bounded, and for long-lived deployments you renew via signed renewals delivered through the same USB image process.
[04:57] Rosa: About hardware — NVLink? We have none in these racks. Should we expect lower throughput?
[05:03] Jamal: Without NVLink you will see higher host-to-host network traffic for shard exchange if you do multi-node sharding. We can optimize for single-node operation where possible, or recommend dedicating hosts for larger models.
[05:16] Dr. Maya: What's the smallest footprint you can run production on?
[05:19] Jamal: For inference-only with quantized 7B and modest batch sizes, a single V100 with 32GB could be ok. For customer safety we recommend at least 48GB of GPU RAM for consistent low-latency. But there are configurations that work on 16–32GB with some perf tradeoffs.
[05:37] Ethan: Auditors also asked about crypto — are signatures FIPS-compliant?
[05:41] Jamal: We support FIPS algorithms and can integrate with FIPS-enabled HSMs. We'll include a configuration note in the security pack.
[05:49] Alyssa: Quick note, we have a compliance dossier and a sample manifest flow. I'll attach both.
[05:54] Dr. Maya: Appreciate it. Another question: what happens if you need to push an urgent security patch and the customer is slow on USB delivery — do you provide a fallback hosted option?
[06:04] Jamal: We can provide emergency remediation guidance. If the site permits a temporary controlled network window we can offer a one-time pull from a pre-authorized IP, but that's policy heavy. For true sealed sites the model is manual delivery; that's why we recommend signed emergency patch images be staged in advance in a secured vault in the facility.
[06:23] Rosa: How about latency expectations? We're concerned about tail latency for short queries used by our LIMS integration.
[06:30] Jamal: In an on-prem setup with local models, tail latency depends on batch size and KV cache. We recommend smaller batch sizes for LIMS (1–2) and an aggressive KV cache warmup. Without cloud routing you'll get consistent low-latency as the runtime sits on local GPUs.
[06:46] Alyssa: Let's talk POC scope — Jamal, what do we propose?
[06:49] Jamal: Proposal: 2-week pilot, 1-node on-site install (your infra team provides host), we deliver signed runtime + quantized 7B model artifact. Tasks: image creation, signing demo, install runbook, run basic perf tests and audit bundle export.
[07:05] Dr. Maya: Will Redwood's SEs be on-site for install?
[07:08] Alyssa: We can offer a paid on-site visit or remote guided install. For sealed environments auditors generally prefer an on-site presence for the first install; we'll include costs in the POC quote.
[07:19] Ethan: About costs — is the POC free?
[07:21] Alyssa: We usually provide a discounted POC with a bill for travel if on-site. The production model would be an enterprise license plus support and optionally reserved capacity pricing if you go dedicated.
[07:33] Rosa: Any client references with similar constraints?
[07:35] Alyssa: We can share anonymized references from two regulated labs who used signed-image delivery and on-prem HSMs; I'll add those contacts in the security pack.
[07:46] Dr. Maya: Ok, practical questions — how is RBAC handled for operator accounts on the node? We need separation between ops and researchers.
[07:53] Jamal: RBAC is enforced at two levels: the runtime has local role definitions for model deploy/read/exec; the admin plane (optional, run in staging) can issue role tokens. For sealed nodes we support local user mapping and signed admin tokens stored in the vault.
[08:07] Ethan: And SSO/SAML?
[08:09] Alyssa: SSO is supported for the Redwood control plane; for Private fully-sealed instances you can integrate SAML with your on-prem identity provider via the staging environment, or use local accounts. We'll document both patterns.
[08:21] Rosa: Let's walk through a sample update flow end-to-end so I can note for infra SOP.
[08:25] Jamal: Sure — step 1: Redwood builds runtime+model artifacts in staging and signs them. Step 2: Signed bundle is delivered to your secured media vault. Step 3: On scheduled patch window, infra loads the image to the host via USB. Node verifies signatures against HSM-stored public key. Step 4: Node performs atomic swap to the updated slot and runs health checks. Step 5: If OK, previous slot is rotated out to a read-only archival partition; if not, automatic rollback occurs. Step 6: Admin exports signed audit bundle for compliance.
[09:01] Dr. Maya: That addresses most of our concerns. One more — can you support offline telemetry collection for internal anomaly detection? We need a format that our SIEM can ingest offline.
[09:11] Jamal: Yes, we can configure structured logs (JSONL) and provide a mapper for your SIEM. Logs are stored encrypted on disk and can be exported as a signed bundle.
[09:20] Alyssa: Ok we're at about 40 minutes, any last blockers?
[09:24] Ethan: I want to make sure the signing keys lifecycle is clear — who holds the private keys?
[09:29] Jamal: Redwood holds the primary signing keys for build artifacts in our KMS; for sealed deployments you have two options: (A) Redwood signs and you validate via a public key in your HSM, or (B) you run a staging signing process where your HSM holds the signing key and both sides verify. Option B is preferred for customers who want full key ownership.
[09:49] Ethan: Option B sounds better for auditors.
[09:52] Dr. Maya: Agreed. If we can keep keys in our control, that reduces audit friction.
[09:58] Alyssa: Understood — we'll include both flows in the security pack. Jamal, anything to add?
[10:02] Jamal: I'll prepare a short demo that shows signing and a simulated rollback. I'll also create a minimal hardware compatibility matrix with recommendations per GPU family.
[10:10] Rosa: I'll get the inventory to you.
[10:12] Dr. Maya: Next steps then?
[10:14] Alyssa: I'll send the security pack, include references and the POC quote. We'll target the SE deep dive the week of 6/28.
[10:20] Ethan: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[10:24] Alyssa: Thanks all — notes and action items will land in email.
